findings.where: Questions, 'Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?' (question 2), steps 2 and 3
findings.what: There are about 21 diamonds. I click maybe 5 or 6, write a few names on the one line and stop. The sheet has no 1775 or 1776 column, so I don't know where 'under the year' is. The siege of Boston runs from 1775 into 1776, so which year does it go under? Step 3 says 'mark who won', but mark it how, and where?
findings.why: This one question could take Jordan 15 minutes or more. He runs out of time before the big question, which is the point of the lesson.
findings.suggestion: Add a small table with two columns, 1775 and 1776, and 4 empty rows in each. New steps: '2. Click 4 diamonds from 1775 and 4 from 1776. Write each battle's name in the right column. If a battle went on into the next year, use the year it started. 3. Next to each name, write A if the Americans won or B if the British won. Check the Legend.'
findings.quote: Click each diamond and write its name under the year it was fought.

findings.what: The port symbols have no names and no pop-ups. I don't know where Charleston or Philadelphia are. 'Use the coastline' doesn't give me a name, so I'd guess or write 'the big dot near New York'. Then step 5 wants me to measure to Philadelphia, and I can't find it.
findings.why: The answer and two of the measurements depend on naming ports Jordan has no way to identify.
findings.suggestion: Give the names on the sheet: 'The major ports on this map are: ______ (list them). Match each big port symbol to a name.' Replace step 4 with: 'Philadelphia is southwest of New York, on a river. Charleston is far to the south, in South Carolina.' If one of the basemaps shows city names, add: 'Change the Basemap to one that shows city names.'
findings.quote: The layer has no pop-ups, so use the coastline and the battle diamonds nearby to name them.

findings.where: Questions, 'Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?' (question 2), Answer
findings.what: The steps get me battle names, but the question asks for colonies. The battle pop-ups don't say which colony a battle is in. Is Quebec a colony? I'd write today's state names if the map shows them, or skip it. 'What changed?' is too open, so I don't know what kind of answer they want.
findings.why: The steps don't collect what the question asks for, so Jordan has to guess or leave it blank.
findings.suggestion: Add a step: '4. To see which colony a battle is in, click the land next to the diamond. Or, if the pop-up says 1 of 2, use the arrows.' Change the question to: 'Name two colonies with battles in 1775 and two with battles in 1776. Did the fighting move north, move south, or stay in one place?'
findings.quote: Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?

findings.where: Questions, 'Where did the war begin?' (question 1), steps 2 and 4 and the Answer
findings.what: The diamonds have no names on the map, so I click around to find Lexington and Concord and 'the Boston diamond'. If I click a different battle near Boston, I copy the wrong dates. Then 'How long did the siege last?' means working out the months between two dates in my head.
findings.why: Wrong dates here carry into the answer. The date maths is a hidden extra step.
findings.suggestion: Step 4: 'Click the diamond in Boston. Check that the pop-up title says Siege of Boston. If it doesn't, try the next diamond or use the arrows.' Answer: 'The siege of Boston started on ________ and ended on ________. That is about ____ months.'
findings.quote: Click the Boston diamond and read its dates.

findings.what: Does 'follow' mean click them? Draw a line? Once I'm zoomed in on New York, circle 5 (Trenton) is probably off the screen in New Jersey. I'd click circle 4 and move on.
findings.why: Circle 5 is the end of the story the big question asks about, and Jordan may never find it.
findings.suggestion: '2. Click circle 4 and read it. Then drag the map down and to the left (southwest) into New Jersey until you see circle 5. Click it and read it.'

findings.where: Questions, 'Where did the war begin?' (question 1), step 5 (first time Measure is used)
findings.what: The sheet never says how Measure works. I click once on Boston and nothing finishes, or I end up on area instead of distance. I'd guess a number.
findings.why: The sheet asks for 5 distances, so if Jordan can't use Measure, all 5 blanks are guesses.
findings.suggestion: Add one how-to line the first time: 'How to measure: open Measure, choose the distance tool, and make sure it says miles. Click once on Boston, then double-click on Concord to finish. Write down the miles.' (Match the button names to the app.)
findings.quote: Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

findings.where: Questions, 'Why New York?' (question 3), Answer, second part
findings.what: 'A navy based at New York' is too abstract for me. I'd write 'the ocean' because I don't know what 'reach' should look like.
findings.why: This is the link to the big question (why New York), and Jordan can't make it.
findings.suggestion: 'Ships could sail from New York along the coast and up the rivers. Name two cities or forts that ships from New York could get to.'
findings.quote: Looking at the map, what could a navy based at New York reach?

findings.what: The layer name is long, and '(inside Revolutionary War Battlefields)' means I have to open another layer to find it. I scroll the layer list, don't see it, and put my hand up.
findings.why: This step gets Jordan stuck before the question even starts.
findings.suggestion: '1. Open Map layers. Click the arrow next to Revolutionary War Battlefields. Turn on Key Port Cities.'
findings.quote: turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (inside Revolutionary War Battlefields).

worksWell: The measure blanks already say 'miles' and have a clear gap, so I know exactly what goes there.
The steps are short, numbered and start with a doing word (Open, Click, Zoom). Question 1 starts with a bookmark, so I land in the right place.
The '1 of 2' tip saves me from missing the second pop-up.

findings.where: Questions, 'The three-fifths clause' (question 3), Answer and the Virginia fill-in line
findings.what: The question wants four numbers: Virginia and South Carolina, each 'counted in full' and 'not at all'. The blank only has Virginia, though, and asks for 'seats with the three-fifths clause', which isn't one of the last two lines I was told to read. There's no blank for South Carolina or for 'in full'. I'd fill in two numbers, maybe wrong ones, and stop.
findings.why: This is the main maths of the lesson. Because the question and the blank don't match, Jordan doesn't know what to write.
findings.suggestion: Use a table that matches the question. Columns: State | House seats in 1793 (three-fifths) | If enslaved people counted in full | If enslaved people not counted. Two rows, Virginia and South Carolina. Change step 2 to: 'Read three lines of the pop-up: House seats in 1793 (this is the three-fifths number), and the last two lines.'

findings.what: The map has no place names, and I'm not sure where Virginia or South Carolina are. I'd click pies until a title says Virginia, which could take a while. If I notice the 'VA' and 'SC' labels from the House seats layer I might guess, but the sheet doesn't tell me to look for them.
findings.why: Every number in this question depends on finding these two states first.
findings.suggestion: '1. Open The South bookmark. Find the labels VA (Virginia) and SC (South Carolina) and click on those states.' (The House seats layer is still on from question 2.)

findings.what: On a map, 'closest' sounds like 'nearest to each other'. Even if I get that it means the vote, I have to subtract for about 14 pies and remember every result. There's nowhere to write them down.
findings.why: The word is easy to misread, and doing the sums in his head is where Jordan gives up.
findings.suggestion: 'Which three states had the closest votes (the smallest gap between votes for and against)? For each pie, take the votes against away from the votes for.' Add a table: State | For | Against | Gap, with 5 rows.

findings.where: Questions, 'Who lived where in 1790?' (question 1), steps 2 and 3 and the Answer
findings.what: That's about 15 pies, and each pop-up is full of numbers. 'More than a quarter' means I have to turn it into 25% myself. By the last pie I've forgotten which ones were over. The sheet doesn't remind me that the biggest pie has the most people (that's buried in the top paragraph).
findings.why: This is slow and the answer is easy to get wrong, all in the first question.
findings.suggestion: Answer: 'Which state had the most people? (Hint: the biggest pie.) Which states had more than 25% (a quarter) of people enslaved?' Add to step 3: 'If the percentage is more than 25%, write the state here: ____________.'
findings.quote: In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved?

findings.where: Questions, 'Seats in Congress' (question 2), Answer, last part
findings.what: The sheet never says Congress has two parts, or that one counts people while the other gives every state the same number. Both my states show 2 senators, but I don't know why that matters. I'd write 'I don't know'.
findings.why: This is the 'balance large and small states' half of the big question, and Jordan has no way in.
findings.suggestion: Add to Before you start: 'Congress has two parts. In the House of Representatives, states with more people get more seats. In the Senate, every state gets 2 senators.' Change the question to: 'Why do you think one part counts people, but the other gives every state the same number?'
findings.quote: Why do you think the House and the Senate are counted differently?

findings.where: Questions, 'The three-fifths clause' (question 3), Answer, last part
findings.what: I wouldn't connect 'people who could not vote' to enslaved people. 'Gained' compared to what? I'd skip it.
findings.why: This is the key idea of the clause, and the wording hides it.
findings.suggestion: 'Which states got more House seats because enslaved people were partly counted? (Look for states where the House seats number is bigger than the not-counted number.)'
findings.quote: Which states gained seats by counting people who could not vote?

findings.what: There's 'House seats in 1793' and also 'House seats today (2020 apportionment)'. I click the first 'House seats' I see. If that's today's layer, I write California or Texas and my answer is for the wrong year.
findings.why: The answer comes out wrong, and nothing on the sheet warns him.
findings.suggestion: '1. In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793. (Not House seats today.)'
findings.quote: In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793.

findings.where: Questions, 'Who lived where in 1790?' (question 1) step 3, and 'How close was ratification?' (question 4) step 3
findings.what: The sheet says the first line gives the percentage enslaved, and in question 4 that it gives the vote. From the map description, the pop-up may list the total, or the result ('ratified'), first. If so, I'd copy the wrong number. I can't tell without the live map.
findings.why: Jordan trusts the sheet exactly, so a wrong line number means a wrong answer.
findings.suggestion: Name the line by what it says, not where it is: 'Find the line that gives the percent enslaved.' and 'Find the line with the vote (__ for, __ against).'
findings.quote: Read the first line of each pop-up, which gives the percentage enslaved.

worksWell: The top paragraph warns me there are no place names and that I can click to see a name. Without that I'd be totally lost.
Question 4 tells me exactly which layers to turn off and on, so the map isn't cluttered.
'Find North Carolina and click both of its pies' is clear, and 'Why does it have two pies?' is a question I can actually answer.
hardWords: counted in full, or not at all

acrossLessons.what: It's one long paragraph packed with what every symbol means. I skip it. Later steps say 'use the legend' or depend on the stripes, the pies or the numbered circles, and I never read what those meant. On We the People, the Maine and West Virginia sentence just confused me.
acrossLessons.why: Jordan gives up on long instructions, so the information he needs most is the part he skips.
acrossLessons.suggestion: Turn it into 4 or 5 short bullets, one per symbol, e.g. 'Diamond = a battle. Its color shows who won (open Legend).' / 'Big pie = more people. Blue = free. Orange-red = enslaved.' Move the Maine and West Virginia note into the question where it's needed, or cut it.
acrossLessons.quote: Diamonds mark battles. A battle's pop-up gives its name, dates and story, but not the winner in words

acrossLessons.where: Both sheets, every 'Answer' with one writing line (e.g. Battles question 1; We the People question 2, which asks 4 things)
acrossLessons.what: Two to four questions share one line. I answer the first one and stop. I can't tell how much to write.
acrossLessons.why: Jordan leaves out half of each answer without realizing it.
acrossLessons.suggestion: Give each part its own line, labeled a, b, c, or a sentence starter, e.g. 'a) Lexington and Concord was fought on ______. ______ won.  b) The siege of Boston lasted ______.'
acrossLessons.quote: Answer: When was Lexington and Concord fought, and who won? How long did the siege of Boston last?

acrossLessons.what: I'd pick 'sketch on the map' to avoid writing. But when I close the tab my sketch is gone, and the teacher never sees it. I'm also not sure what counts as 'evidence from two places' or 'two layers'.
acrossLessons.why: Jordan could hand in nothing for the main task.
acrossLessons.suggestion: 'Answer the big question in 3 or 4 sentences. Name two places on the map (or two layers) and say what each one shows. If you sketch on the map, take a screenshot and hand it in.'
acrossLessons.quote: You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

acrossLessons.what: I estimate 65 minutes for Battles and 60 for We the People. The big question comes last, so I never reach it in a 45 to 50 minute class.
acrossLessons.why: Jordan does the clicking and misses the thinking.
acrossLessons.suggestion: Mark one question per sheet as 'If you have time', or cut the 'click every diamond / every pie' steps down to a set number (e.g. 'Click 4 pies').
acrossLessons.quote: Click the pies and read each pop-up.

acrossLessons.what: The questions have no numbers. If my teacher says 'do question 3', I can't find it. If '(numbered)' really prints after each heading, I'd think it's an instruction.
acrossLessons.why: Small thing, but it costs time and gets Jordan lost on the page.
acrossLessons.suggestion: 'Question 1: Where did the war begin?' Remove '(numbered)' if it shows on the printed sheet.

acrossLessons.what: 'From reading alone' — reading what? We didn't read anything else in this lesson. I'd write 'it was a map'.
acrossLessons.why: This is a weak finish because the question needs a comparison Jordan doesn't have.
acrossLessons.suggestion: 'What is one thing the map showed you that you wouldn't get from just reading a list of dates or numbers?'
acrossLessons.quote: that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

acrossLessons.what: In this text version there's only the map's title, with no link or short web address. If the printed sheet is the same, I don't know how to open it and I wait for the teacher.
acrossLessons.why: This is the first step, and if it fails Jordan can't start at all.
acrossLessons.suggestion: Add a short link or QR code next to the title: 'Open the map: [short link]'.
